title: Gateway, integration, backend: what goes where
summary: Three layers with three different jobs, and the rules that keep them apart.

steps.title: Three layers, three jobs
body: A consumer never talks to a backend directly. The request crosses two layers first:
```text
consumer ──► API gateway ──► integration ──► backend
(token)    who? how often?   how to talk     business rules
to backends     and data
| Layer | Owns | Examples |
| **Gateway** | Who may call and how often | tokens, API keys, subscriptions, scopes, rate limits, quotas, TLS, analytics, developer portal |
| **Integration** | How to talk to backends | routing, protocol bridging, transforming data, combining several calls, mapping errors, retries, adding backend credentials |
| **Backend** | What the business does | prices, stock rules, order state, the database |
In .NET terms: the gateway is like Azure API Management in front of your services; the integration layer is
like an ASP.NET Core service using `HttpClient`, a mapper and Polly, but assembled from ready-made components.

items: Reject calls without a valid token
Allow 100 requests per minute per partner
Call the catalogue and the warehouse, then merge the answers
Add the carrier's secret API key to outgoing calls
Decide whether a customer qualifies for free delivery
Store the order in the database

steps.title: Three rules
body: 1. **Never rely on the integration layer alone for security.** The gateway enforces who may call. The
integration still validates input (defence in depth), but it is not the lock on the front door.
2. **Never hide business transformation inside the gateway.** Gateway policies are configuration in a
product's UI; they are rarely code-reviewed or unit-tested. Mapping and orchestration belong in the
integration layer, in Git, with tests.
3. **A pure pass-through needs no integration layer.** If a backend already speaks a clean contract,
publish it on the gateway directly. Every extra hop costs latency and something else to run.
Business rules belong in neither: they live in the backend that owns the data.

steps.prompt: A team proposes computing loyalty discounts in a script inside the API gateway, "because every request passes through it anyway". What is the best answer?
options: No: discount rules are business logic and belong in the backend that owns orders and prices
Yes: the gateway sees every request, so it is the most efficient place
Yes, as long as the script is short
No: put it in the integration layer's error handler instead
steps.explain: The gateway is for access and traffic policy. Business rules hidden in a gateway script are invisible to the team that owns pricing, hard to test and hard to version.

steps.prompt: An old bus "secured" an API by checking that a `X-Client-Name` header was present. What is wrong with that?
options: Anyone can send any header; presence of a header proves nothing about who the caller is
Nothing, header checks are standard authentication
It should have checked the `User-Agent` header instead
steps.explain: Authentication needs a secret or a signed credential the caller cannot invent: an API key, an OAuth2 token, a client certificate. Checking it is the gateway's job.

steps.title: Layers as functions
body: Each layer can be modelled as a function that takes a request and returns a response, wrapping the next layer.
It is exactly how ASP.NET Core middleware works.
```csharp
delegate Res Handler(Req r);
Handler Gateway(Handler next) => r =>
r.Headers.ContainsKey("Authorization") ? next(r) : new Res(401, "unauthorized");
Handler app = Gateway(Integration(Backend));
The gateway can answer on its own (401, 403, 429) and the call never reaches anything behind it.

code: Func<string?, int> backend = token => { calls++; return 200; };
Func<string?, int> gateway = token => token == "good" ? backend(token) : 401;
steps.explain: Rejected calls stop at the gateway. That protects every system behind it from load and from unauthenticated traffic.

steps.prompt: Put one request's journey in order.
lines: The consumer app asks the key manager for a token (client credentials)
It calls the gateway with `Authorization: Bearer <token>`
The gateway checks the token, the subscription, the scope and the rate limit
The gateway removes the consumer's token and forwards the call to the integration
The integration calls the backend, transforms the answer and maps any error
The response travels back; both layers log the same correlation id
steps.explain: Each layer does its own job once. Notice that the consumer's token never reaches the backend.

steps.title: A gateway in front
prompt: The tests declare these types (you don't write them):
record Req(string Path, Dictionary<string, string> Headers);
Write `Handler Gateway(Handler next, HashSet<string> validTokens)` that returns a handler which:
- answers `new Res(401, "unauthorized")` when there is no `Authorization` header, it does not start with `Bearer `, or the token after it is not in `validTokens`;

- otherwise calls `next` with a **new** `Req`: same path, a **copy** of the headers **without** `Authorization` (the consumer's token must not reach the backend). Don't change the caller's dictionary.
Header names are case-insensitive: build the copy with `StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase`.
solution: var headers = new Dictionary<string, string>(r.Headers, StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
hints: `new Dictionary<string, string>(r.Headers, StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase)` copies the headers; then `Remove("Authorization")`.
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoSeen = new List<Req>();
Handler dojoBackend = r => { dojoSeen.Add(r); return new Res(200, "book " + r.Path); };
var dojoApp = Gateway(dojoBackend, new HashSet<string> { "t-123" });
Dictionary<string, string> H(params (string, string)[] kv)
var d = new Dictionary<string, string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
foreach (var (k, v) in kv) d[k] = v;
return d;
Dojo.Eq("no Authorization header -> 401", 401, dojoApp(new Req("/books/1", H())).Status);
Dojo.Eq("Basic scheme -> 401", 401, dojoApp(new Req("/books/1", H(("Authorization", "Basic abc")))).Status);
Dojo.Eq("unknown token -> 401", 401, dojoApp(new Req("/books/1", H(("Authorization", "Bearer nope")))).Status);
Dojo.Eq("rejected calls never reach the backend", 0, dojoSeen.Count);
var dojoIn = H(("Authorization", "Bearer t-123"), ("X-Trace-Id", "abc"));
var dojoOk = dojoApp(new Req("/books/1", dojoIn));
Dojo.Eq("valid token -> backend answers 200", 200, dojoOk.Status);
Dojo.Eq("backend got the same path", "/books/1", dojoSeen.Count == 1 ? dojoSeen[0].Path : "");
Dojo.Check("backend did not receive Authorization", dojoSeen.Count == 1 && !dojoSeen[0].Headers.ContainsKey("authorization"), "the token leaked to the backend");
Dojo.Check("other headers are kept", dojoSeen.Count == 1 && dojoSeen[0].Headers.ContainsKey("X-Trace-Id"), "X-Trace-Id was lost");
Dojo.Check("the caller's dictionary is unchanged", dojoIn.ContainsKey("Authorization"), "you removed the header from the caller's own dictionary");
record Req(string Path, Dictionary<string, string> Headers);
record Res(int Status, string Body);
delegate Res Handler(Req r);
